name: Creamy Roasted Garlic Chicken

ingredients.buy: 3 1/2 tbsp, for dusting the cutlets; 10 1/2 tbsp

writer_notes: Completed slug: creamy-roasted-garlic-chicken. All 10 bought lines are used by a step and no step calls for anything unbought. Chicken (steps 3, 4, 7), butter (searing step 4 plus the roux in sauce step 6), olive oil (step 4), salt (season the cutlets step 3 plus season the sauce step 6), black pepper (steps 3 and 6), all-purpose flour (dusting the cutlets step 3 plus the roux step 6), garlic (roasted in step 2, mashed into the sauce step 6), milk (step 6), parmesan (step 6), hot sauce (optional finish, step 6). Walked the costed list against the steps in both directions.

SOURCE STEPS name two ingredients the build does NOT buy: Italian seasoning (source step 2) and a parsley garnish (source step 7). Neither is on the shopper's list, so I dropped both from the prose rather than write a step that uses something nobody purchased. Both are in forbidden_prose_terms.

NO heavy cream in this recipe: the creamy sauce is milk (1715 g, 7 cups) thickened with a butter-and-flour roux and finished with parmesan. The prose leans on the milk-not-cream contrast as the budget angle, but no cream, half-and-half, or cream cheese is bought or named as an ingredient. I did NOT put 'heavy cream' in forbidden_prose_terms because I deliberately reference it to say it is absent.

prose.intro_html: Creamy garlic chicken sounds like something you order out and pay restaurant money for, but look down the list and there is not a drop of heavy cream in it. The sauce gets its body from milk, a spoon of flour, and a fistful of garlic that turns sweet and mellow when you roast it in a dry pan. You sear seasoned cutlets, build a simple white sauce right behind them, and stir in parmesan until it clings to every piece. Built at 14 servings it runs about {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein a serving, with about 15 grams of carbs, for roughly ${{cost_ps}} a serving (at everyday cost). That is a rich, garlicky dinner that eats like a splurge and shops like a Tuesday.
shop_smart: The big pack of breasts is the whole game. Seven pounds of boneless skinless breast is where nearly all the money and all the protein sit. Reach for the family value pack instead of the little trays so you are buying chicken and not shrink wrap, and slice the thick breasts flat into cutlets yourself. When breast hits a sale price, grab extra and freeze it in batch-size bags.

Milk is the trick here, not cream. This creamy sauce is built on plain milk thickened with butter and flour, so you skip the pricey little carton of heavy cream entirely. You only need about seven cups, but the gallon is still the play: by the ounce it beats the half gallon, and the leftover milk goes straight onto your cereal.

Buy your garlic by the head, not the jar. This dish leans on roasted garlic, about three and a half heads of it, and roasting whole cloves in a dry pan is what turns them sweet instead of sharp. Loose fresh heads are cheap and roast up far better than the pre-minced jar, which would just scorch.

Grab the grated parmesan. It melts straight into the sauce, so whichever grated tub or bag is cheapest is the right one. There is no reason to chase an expensive wedge when it is going to disappear into a white sauce anyway.

Butter, flour, oil, salt, and pepper carry the rest. A little butter and oil to sear and to start the sauce, flour to dust the chicken and to thicken the pan, and salt and pepper to taste. These are backbone staples you most likely already own, so they barely move the cart. A few dashes of hot sauce at the end is optional if you want a little heat.
make_it: Weigh your empty skillet and write the number down. You will use it at the end to split this into 14 even servings by weight instead of eyeballing every container.

Break the garlic heads into individual cloves, skins still on, and add them to a dry skillet over medium heat. Cook about 15 minutes, stirring to turn and brown them, until the cloves are soft inside even if the skins darken. Let them cool, then peel or squeeze the cloves out and mash them smooth with the side of your knife. Set aside.
Slice each chicken breast flat into cutlets. Season both sides with salt and black pepper, then dust each side lightly with flour and set the cutlets aside.

In a large skillet over medium-high heat, melt part of the butter with the olive oil. Working in batches so the pan is not crowded, sear the cutlets a few minutes a side until golden and cooked through (165F in the thickest part). Move the chicken to a plate and cover it with foil to keep warm.
Lower the heat to medium and add the rest of the butter to the same pan, scraping up all the browned bits stuck to the bottom.

Whisk the flour into the butter and cook a couple of minutes. Slowly whisk in the milk until the sauce is smooth, then stir in the mashed roasted garlic and the parmesan and cook, whisking, until the sauce thickens. Season with salt and pepper to taste, and stir in the hot sauce now if you want a little heat.
Return the chicken and any collected juices to the pan and spoon the sauce over every cutlet to coat.

Weigh the full pan and subtract the empty weight from Step 1 to get the cooked total. Divide by 14 and give each container one cutlet and an even share of the roasted garlic sauce, aiming for that weight.
prose.portion_html: Set the full pan on your scale and subtract the empty weight you wrote down in Step 1 to get the cooked total. Divide that number by 14. Each container gets one chicken cutlet and an even ladle of the roasted garlic parmesan sauce, landing near {{cal}} calories with {{protein}} grams of protein.
prose.cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a serving (at everyday cost) for a creamy roasted garlic chicken that tastes like it cost three times that. The chicken and the milk-based sauce carry it, and the roasted garlic does the expensive-tasting work for pennies.

steps: Break the garlic into cloves, skins on, and roast them in a dry skillet over medium heat about 15 minutes until soft, then cool, peel, and mash smooth.
Slice the chicken breasts into cutlets, season both sides with salt and black pepper, and dust with flour.
Sear the cutlets in butter and olive oil until golden and cooked through, then set them aside and keep warm.
In the same pan, cook the flour in butter, whisk in the milk until smooth, then stir in the roasted garlic and parmesan and season, adding hot sauce if you like heat.
Spoon the sauce over the chicken, then weigh, divide, and portion into 14 containers.
